lesson.title: Beyond the Number Line: An Introduction to Complex Numbers
lesson.summary: Complex numbers extend the real numbers by defining i as the square root of negative one, giving every polynomial equation a solution and letting you do arithmetic with numbers that have both a real and an imaginary part.
lesson.body:
Every real number squares to a value that is zero or positive, which means an equation like x² = -1 has no solution among the real numbers. Mathematicians resolved this gap by defining a new number, i, with the property i² = -1 (equivalently, i = √-1). A complex number is then any number of the form a + bi, where a is called the real part and b is called the imaginary part, both ordinary real numbers. This is not a trick or an approximation: complex numbers form a complete, consistent number system, and they show up in genuinely practical settings such as electrical engineering, signal processing, and the mathematics behind quantum mechanics.

Adding and subtracting complex numbers is done component by component, combining real parts with real parts and imaginary parts with imaginary parts, similar to combining like terms in algebra: (3 + 4i) + (2 - i) = 5 + 3i. Multiplying complex numbers uses the distributive property (FOIL), just like multiplying two binomials, with one extra step: whenever i² appears, replace it with -1. Here is a fully worked multiplication example. Multiply (3 + 4i)(2 - i). Distributing gives 3(2) + 3(-i) + 4i(2) + 4i(-i) = 6 - 3i + 8i - 4i². Combining the imaginary terms, -3i + 8i = 5i, and replacing i² with -1 turns -4i² into -4(-1) = 4. So the product is 6 + 5i + 4 = 10 + 5i.

Dividing complex numbers requires eliminating i from the denominator, which is done by multiplying both the numerator and denominator by the denominator's complex conjugate. The conjugate of a + bi is a - bi, and the two multiply to a real number: (a + bi)(a - bi) = a² + b², since the middle terms cancel and i² becomes -1. For example, to compute (3 + 4i)/(1 - i), multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator, 1 + i: the denominator becomes (1 - i)(1 + i) = 1² + 1² = 2, and the numerator becomes (3 + 4i)(1 + i) = 3 + 3i + 4i + 4i² = 3 + 7i - 4 = -1 + 7i. The quotient is (-1 + 7i)/2, which can also be written -1/2 + (7/2)i.

The modulus (or absolute value) of a complex number a + bi measures its distance from the origin when plotted on the complex plane, where the horizontal axis represents the real part and the vertical axis represents the imaginary part. It is calculated with the same distance-formula logic as the Pythagorean theorem: |a + bi| = √(a² + b²). For 3 + 4i, the modulus is √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5, the same 3-4-5 relationship you'd recognize from a right triangle. One more pattern worth memorizing is that powers of i cycle with period 4: i¹ = i, i² = -1, i³ = -i, and i⁴ = 1, after which the cycle repeats, so any higher power of i can be simplified by finding the remainder when the exponent is divided by 4.
